title: Section 1: Euclids Algorithm
text: Within this weeks lesson, we are going to learn an important algorithm which can be used in more advanced cryptography work, however I am going to try and keep it simple. Then we will look at how to find the modular inverse of a number, which can be used to break an affine cipher. Lastly, we will look at a method which can be used to break any monoalphabetic substitution cipher (which include shift ciphers and affine ciphers).

title: Section 1: Euclids Algorithm
text:
(Difficulty: 3/5)

Who is Euclid?
We will start with a little bit of history about Euclid. Euclid was an ancient Greek Mathematician, who is known as the ‘father of geometry’ due to his study of shapes. He was the first Mathematician who wrote things called ‘axioms’, which you can think of as rules that Maths has to follow. This means he was very important to the development of Mathematics. I would recommend having a little read about him (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid).











What is an algorithm?
‘Algorithm’=‘алгоритм’ An algorithm is a set of instructions which are used to solve a specific problem. They are quite common in Computer Science and Mathematics. You can think of it as like a cooking recipe, if you follow all the instructions correctly and have all the right ingredients, then you will get some wonderful food.


What is Euclids Algorithm?
Euclids algorithm is used to find the greatest common divisor between two numbers. So far we have only used small numbers. For example, we can easily see that the greatest common divisor between 27 and 33 is 3. However, as we use larger numbers, it is going to be harder to find their prime factors meaning it’s harder to find their greatest common divisors. Just as a reminder, if the greatest common divisor of two numbers \(x\) and \(y\) is \(z\), then I would write \(gcd(x,y)=z\). For example, \(gcd(27,33)=3\).
If I asked you to find the greatest common divisor of 10302 and 21726, you might find the answer but it would take a lot of time. Euclids algorithm gives you a quick method. However, before looking at \(gcd(10302,21726)\), we are going to use an easier example to get you familiar with the algorithm.
Before we start the examples, I would like to credit this youtube video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jwf6ncRmhPg). This is the video explains Euclids algorithm very well, and it’s what gave me the idea to represent Euclids algorithm in the way that you’re about to see in the examples. So give it a watch after doing the examples.


Example 1
For this example, each slide represents one of the steps below, so click through the slides and read what they mean at each step.
Find \(gcd(78,102)\) using Euclids Algorithm.
Steps:

First, I want you to imagine that we have got each number in its own area, like what is being shown in the diagram. We can see that there is 78 dots on the left, and 102 dots on the right.
We then look at whichever area has the most amount of dots in, and take away the number of dots from the other side as many times as we can. For this example, we can only take 78 away from 102 once, because if we did it twice then we would have a negative number.
You then write out the new number of dots that you have in each side. We now have 78 does on the left side, and 24 dots on the right side (as \(102-78=24\)).
We then repeat step 2. We can see that now 78 is the side with the most dots, so we take away 24 from 78 for as many times as we can. We take three lots of 24 away from 78, because if we took 4 lots away, then we would have a negative number.
We now have 6 dots on the left side, and 24 dots on the right side.
We can now do our last step, and take away 4 lots of 6 from the right side, to leave us with zero.
We are left with 6 and 0, meaning that the greatest common divisor of 78 and 102 is 6. Our answer is \(gcd(78,102)=6\).


  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 7
    Next ▶
  





Now that you have seen an example, it’s time for me to explain some things. - The number on the left and the number on the right will always have the same greatest common divisor. - One of the ways the algorithm ends is by getting a zero in one of the areas. This means that the \(gcd\) is equal to whatever number is in the other box. - The other way the algorithm ends is by getting a one in one of the areas. This means that the \(gcd\) of the two numbers is equal to one (hence the numbers are coprime).
We will now look at an example where the two numbers are coprime, so you can see what happens.


Example 2
Similar to the last example, please click through the slideshow and read through the steps so you know what is happening on each slide.
Find \(gcd(82,65)\) using Euclids Algorithm.
Steps:

Write our two numbers in their two seperate areas.
Notice that 82 is the larger number, so we take away 65 from 82 as many times as we can before we get a negative number. We only take 65 away once, because if we took it away twice then we would get a negative number.
Our new numbers are 17 and 65.
We can see that 65 is now the larger number so we take away 17 from 65. This time, we can only take 17 away from 65 3 times before getting a negative number.
Now we are left with 17 and 14.
17 is our larger number, so we take 14 away from it.
We are left with 3 and 14.
14 is our larger number, so we take 3 away from it.
We are left with 3 and 2.
3 is our larger number so we take 2 away from it.
We are left with 1 and 2. I said earlier that the algorithm ends when we get either a 1 or a zero, and now that we have a 1, we end our algorithm.


  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 11
    Next ▶
  



For this example, we can see that we get 1 as one of our final numbers. This means that \(gcd(82,65)=1\), so 82 and 65 are coprime.
When you see these examples, you might think to yourself that I am doing a lot of work for these questions, and you would be right. I am showing you every step that is needed to get the correct answer. However, once you have some practice with these questions then you will be able to do them a lot quicker. In example 2, at step 5 we had 17 and 14 in our two boxes. If you remember that the greatest common divisor of the two numbers in the boxes will always be the same, then you can realise that \(gcd(82,65)=gcd(17,14)\). You might also notice that 17 is a prime number, and the greatest common divisor between a prime number and any other number (except the prime itself) is equal to 1. So you would have been able to stop the algorithm after the 5th step as you would already know that the two numbers had a greatest common divisor of one.
Anyway, it’s time for one last example, but this time we are going to use some big numbers to show you how useful this algorithm is.


Example 3
Find \(gcd(10302,21726)\) using Euclids Algorithm.
As you can see these numbers are quite large, and I do not have the time to create a diagram with twenty thousand dots in, so we are going to do this without a diagram. The algorithm will stay exactly the same, only you will not have the visual help. If you are struggling to understand what is happening without the diagrams, then I recommend having a go at some of the easier practice questions first, then come back to this example.
The first thing we are going to do is take away the smaller number from the larger number as many times as possible. We can see that \(21726\) is larger than \(10302\), so we will do: \[21726-2 \times 10302 = 1122\]
Our new numbers are now, \(10302\) and \(1122\). This means that we do: \[10302- 9 \times 1122=204\]
Our new numbers are now, \(204\) and \(1122\). We now carry on the process and take the smaller number away from the larger one: \[1122- 5 \times 204 = 102\]
Now we have our two numbers as \(204\) and \(102\). Lastly, we can see that: \[204 - 2 \times 102 = 0\] Meaning that the algorithm ends because we have got a zero.
Our final answer is that \(gcd(10302,21726)=102\). I hope you can appreciate that without Euclids algorithm, it would have been very difficult to spot that \(102\) is a factor of both \(10302\) and \(21726\), which shows you how useful this algorithm is.
Some of you may have realised that at the begining I said an algorithm was a set of instructions to solve a problem, however I never explicitly gave you the instructions for this algorithm. I did this because I did not want to confuse you, as it does look a bit difficult if you have never seen it before. Hopefully now you are familiar with some examples, you will be able to understand the instructions easier. The instructions are as follows:

Start with two numbers \(x\) and \(y\) where $x y > 0 $.
Divide \(x\) by \(y\) to get two numbers \(q\) and \(r\) such that: \[x = y \times q + r\] Where \(0 \leq r < y\).
Check the remainder:

if \(r=0\), then \(y\) is the greatest common divisor.
if \(r\) is not equal to zero, replace \(x\) with \(y\) and \(y\) with \(r\), then go back to step 2.


Also, according to these instructions, you only end the algorithm if you have zero as one of you numbers, however I said that you end the algorithm if you have either a zero or a one. Both of these methods will work, because if you see a \(1\) as one of your numbers, then you know on the next step you will have a zero anyways (because every number, \(n\), can be wrote as \(n = n \times 1\)), so my method saves a little bit of time.
Hopefully, you’re familiar with this algorithm now, as it is time for some practice questions!

title: Section 1: Euclids Algorithm
text:
(Difficulty: 4/5)
Within this section we will be looking at how to find what \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) someone has used in an affine cipher, if you know that ciphertext and the plaintext.
We will be looking at some rather difficult Maths, as we will be adding to our knowledge of Euclids Algorithm by introducing the Extended Euclidian Algorithm. We will also introduce the concept of multiplicative modular inverses (I know it sounds scary, but trust me when I say that it’s not that bad).

What is a multiplicative inverse?
Every number has a multiplicative inverse. If I have a number \(x\), then its multiplicative inverse is the number \(y\) such that: \[x \times y = 1\]
For normal numbers (when we are not using mod), this is very easy to calculate. For example, the multiplicative inverse of \(2\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\). We can check this and see that: \[2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1\]
The multiplicative inverse of \(60\) is \(\frac{1}{60}\), because: \[60 \times \frac{1}{60} = 1\]
The multiplicative inverse of \(-\frac{1}{5}\) is \(-5\), because: \[-\frac{1}{5} \times -5 = 1\]
I could carry on doing these examples, but I think you probably get the idea. For any number \(x\), the multiplicative inverse is \(\frac{1}{x}\), so you don’t even need to do any Maths, you can simply write the same number underneath \(1\) in a fraction.
For a little bit more information, ‘multiplicative’ means that we are multiplying the numbers together (as you can probably guess), and ‘inverse’ means that they equal one. If you study Maths futher you will find that this links heavily with group theory, however we will not look at that now (maybe I will do a course on it in the future, if you are interested).
You can also say that if we have some number \(x\), then its modular inverse is \(x^{-1}\) such that: \[x \times x^{-1} = 1\] This is exactly the same as the other definition, only I have swapped \(y\) with \(x^{-1}\).


What is a modular multiplicative inverse?
Note that for this section I have used \(\text{mod 26}\) for the examples, however they will still work if you use another number.
Similar to the last part, we still need two numbers to multiply together to equal one, however the difference is that now we are using modular arithmetic. If I have a number \(x\), then its modular multiplicative inverse under modulo \(26\) is the number \(y\) such that: \[x \times y = 1 \text{ (mod 26)}\]
It can sometimes be very difficult to find the number \(y\), however we have some tricks we can use.
First, we know that \(\text{mod}\) is hard to deal with, so we need to find a way to get rid of it. We can remember that when we have \(\text{mod 26}\) at the end of an equation, all it means is that we are adding (or subtracking) some multiple of \(26\) from either side of the equation. This means that we do this:\[x \times y = 1 \text{ (mod 26)} \implies x \times y + 26 \times n = 1\] where \(n\) is just an integer.
Please take some time to make sure that you understand the step above. We will use the Extended Euclidian Algorithm to solve the equation above.


What is the Extended Euclidian Algorithm?
The Extended Euclidian Algorithm is an algorithm used to find \(gcd(a,b)\) of two numbers \(a\) and \(b\), then it finds the integers \(x\) and \(y\) such that: \[a \times x + b \times y = gcd(a,b)\]
The first thing to notice is that the first half of this algorithm is exactly the same as the Euclidian Algorithm! The Euclidian Algorithm is used to find the greatest common divisor of two number \(a\) and \(b\), so you already know how to use half of this algorithm. We will now look at this algorithm in an example.


Example 1
Use the Extended Euclidian Algorithm on the numbers \(35\) and \(29\).
The first half of this algorithm is just the Euclidian Algorithm, and we know how that works. Using Euclids algorithm, we get: \[35=29 \times 1 + 6\] \[29= 6 \times 4 + 5\] \[6 = 5 \times 1 + 1 \] \[5 = 1 \times 5 + 0\]
The algorithm has finished with \(0\) and \(1\) being the final numbers. This shows that \(gcd(35,29)=1\), so \(35\) and \(29\) are coprime.
We use Euclids Algorithm to change two large numbers into smaller numbers while keeping the \(gcd\) between the numbers the same. This makes it easier to work out the \(gcd\). With the Extended Euclidian Algorithm, we change smaller numbers into larger numbers, while still requiring the difference between the numbers to be equal to one.
In the slideshow below, I will be getting a lot of equations our of seemingly nowhere. However, all of the equations I get are simply the ones above but they have been rearranged. This is why we need to do the Euclidian Algorithm first. Rearranging the equations above, we can get:\[35=29 \times 1 + 6 \implies 35 - 29 \times 1 = 6\] \[29= 6 \times 4 + 5 \implies 29 - 6 \times 4 = 5\] \[6 = 5 \times 1 + 1 \implies 6-5 \times 1 =1\]
This next slideshow now goes through the Extended Euclidian Algorithm for this specific example. I have used a lot of slides to break it up into smaller parts making it easier to understand.

  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 25
    Next ▶
  



This give us our final equation of: \[35 \times 5 - 29 \times 6 =1 \]
This tells us that: \[35 \times 5 - 29 \times 6 = 1 \implies 29 \times 6 =1 \text{ (mod 35)}\]
Now we are going to look at another example, this time in the context of an affine cipher.


Example 2
My affine cipher uses the English alphabet and maps the plaintext letter ‘P’ to the ciphertext letter ‘T’, and the plaintext letter ‘V’ to the ciphertext letter ‘H’. What \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) have I used?
My first step is to convert the information above into equations. We know that an affine cipher has the form: \[ \text{Ciphertext} = \text{Plaintext} \times \alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Now converting our letters into numbers, we get: \[\text{P,V,T,V} = 15,21,19,7\]
Now we can put these numbers into our affine cipher equation, to get two equations to solve. Make sure to not get confused between the ciphertext and plaintext! When we do that we should get: \[19 = 15 \alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\] \[7 = 21 \alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Now we are going to take the first equation away from the second equation to give us: \[-12 = 6 \alpha \text{ (mod 26)}\]
To get rid of the negative, I’m going to add \(26\) to the left hand side. I can do this because the equation is under \(\text{mod 26}\). I then get: \[14 = 6 \alpha \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We see that both sides of this equation are divisible by 2, so we can divide both sides by 2 to give us: \[ 7 = 3 \alpha \text{ (mod 26)}\]
To solve this equation we need to get the \(\alpha\) by itself, which we can do by getting rid of the \(3\). Normally, we would divide both sides of the equation by \(3\), however doing this would give a non-integer value of \(\alpha\) which we know is not possible. This is where the modular multiplicative inverse comes in. We want to find some number that, when multiplied by \(3\), will give \(1\). In other words, we want to solve this equation: \[3 \times x = 1 \text{ (mod 26)}\] Which is the same as: \[ 3x + 26n = 1\] where \(n\) is an integer.
And we can solve this by using the Extended Euclidian Algorithm.
The first step is to complete the normal Euclidian Algorithm for the numbers \(3\) and \(26\). Doing this we will get: \[26 = 3 \times 8 +2\] \[3 = 2 \times 1 +1 \] \[2 = 2 \times 1 +0 \]
This has confirmed that \(3\) and \(26\) are coprime, but it also sets up our next step. In this next step, we are going to re-arrange the equation \(3= 2 \times 1 + 1\), so we have \(1\) as the subject of the equation. Doing this we have: \[ 3 = 2 \times 1 + 1 \implies 1 = 3 - 2 \times 1\]
Now we can use our first equation (\(26 = 3 \times 8 + 2\)), to express \(1\) in terms of \(3\) and \(26\). We can do this by re-arranging it into \(2=26 - 3 \times 8\), and substitute this into our expression for \(1\). We get: \[1= 3-2 \times 1 \implies 1 = 3 - (26 - 3 \times 8) \times 1\]
Simplifying this, we get: \[ 1 = 3 \times 9 - 26 \times 1\]
This is the end of our Extended Euclidian Algorithm, as we now have an equation in the form,\(x \times y + 26 \times n = 1\). We have \(x=9\). From this equation, we can bring back our \(\text{mod 26}\), which will give us the equation: \[ 3 \times 9 = 1 \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We have now found our modular multiplicative inverse! The inverse of \(3\) is \(9\), because \(3\) multiplied by \(9\) will give you \(1\) in \(\text{mod 26}\). This means we can go back to our equation with \(\alpha\), and solve it for \(\alpha\). Just as a reminder, our equation we are trying to solve is: \[7 = 3 \alpha \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We can now multiply both sides of the equation by \(9\) (because that is the inverse of \(3\)), to give us: \[ 9 \times 7 = 9 \times 3 \alpha \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 63 = \alpha \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 11 = \alpha \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Finally, we have our value of \(\alpha\). Now the last thing we need to do is find our value of \(\beta\) to finish this question. We can do this by using one of the equations with our plaintext and ciphertext in, substitute in \(\alpha\), and then solve for \(\beta\). We will use the equation: \[19 = 15\alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Substituting in our value for \(\alpha\), we get: \[ 19 = 15 \times 11 + \beta \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 19 = 165 + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
The with a bit of re-arranging we will get:\[ 19 = 165 + \beta \text{ (mod 26)} \implies -146 = \beta \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 10 = \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
This gives up our final values of \(\alpha = 11\) and \(\beta = 10\). You can check to see if they are correct, by encrypting the plaintext using these values and seeing what you get as the ciphertext. I would recommend doing that when you have a go at some practice questions.
Now as this is difficult Maths, I am going to go through another example before giving you some practice questions. If you felt confident with example 2, then I would recommend having a go at example 3 before looking at how I did it. It’s a good way to test your work.


Example 3
My affine cipher uses the Ukrainian alphabet and maps the plaintext letter ‘ъ’ onto the ciphertext letter ‘о’, and the plaintext letter ‘н’ onto the ciphertext letter ‘ш’. What value of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) have I used?
Like in the previous example, we need to convert these letters into numbers, and we do this by using the equation, \(\text{Ciphertext}=\text{Plaintext}\times \alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 33)}\). We know that: \[ \text{ъ}=30,\text{о}=18,\text{н}=17,\text{ш}=28\]
Using our Ukrainian alphabet to number converter. Now we can substitute these into our equation for an affine cipher. This will give us the two equations: \[ 18 = 30 \alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 33)}\] \[28= 17 \alpha + \beta \text{ (mod 33)}\]
We can subtract these equations away from each other to get rid of \(\beta\). This will give us: \[ -10 = 13 \alpha \text{ (mod 33)} \implies 23 = 13 \alpha \text{ (mod 33)}\]
Now we need to be able to get the \(\alpha\) by itself. We can do this by finding the modular multiplicative inverse of \(13\) in \(\text{mod 33}\). In other words, we want to find a value for \(x\), such that: \[1 = 13x \text{ (mod 33)}\]
This means we need to use the Extended Euclidian Algorithm. We first use the Euclidian algorithm, as follows: \[33 = 2 \times 13 +7 \] \[13 = 7 \times 1 + 6\] \[ 7 = 6 \times 1 +1 \] \[6 = 1\times 6 +0\]
This also confirms that \(13\) and \(33\) are coprime. Now we can use the 2nd part of the Extended Euclidian Algorithm. By re-arranging the equation \(7 = 6 \times 1 + 1\), we can get an equation which equals one. We get: \[ 1 = 7 - 6 \times 1\]
Now we can represent \(6\) in terms of \(7\) and \(13\) by the equation $13= 7 + 6 $. Substituting in our equation for \(6\), we get:\[ 1 = 7 - 6 \times 1 \implies 1 = 7 - (13-7\times 1) \times 1\]
Grouping the \(7\)s together, we get: \[ 1= 2 \times 7 - 13 \times 1\]
Now we can represent \(7\) in terms of \(13\) and \(33\) by the equation \(33=2\times 13 +7\). Substituting in our equation for \(7\), we get: \[1 = 2 \times 7 - 13 \times 1 \implies 1 = 2 \times (33 - 2 \times 13) - 13 \times 1\]
Expanding the brackets and grouping all of our \(13\)s together will give us: \[1 = 33 \times 2 - 13 \times 5\]
Which tells us that: \[ 1 = 13 \times -5 \text{ (mod 33)}\]
But we can convert \(-5\) into a positive number by adding \(33\) thirteen times to the right side of the equation (remember because we are dealing in \(\text{mod 33}\) we can add any multiple of \(33\) to the equation and it remains the same). This gives us: \[1=13 \times 28 \text{ (mod 33)}\]
So our value of \(x\) is 28. Meaning the modular multiplicative inverse of \(13\) under \(\text{mod 33}\) is \(28\).
Now we can solve our equation \(23 = 13 \alpha \text{ (mod 33)}\). We do this by multiplying both sides of the equation by \(28\). This will give us:\[28\times 23 = 28 \times 13 \alpha \text{ (mod 33)} \implies 644 = \alpha \text{ (mod 33)} \implies 17 = \alpha\]
Now that we have our value for \(\alpha\), our last step is to find our value of \(\beta\). We can do this by using one of our equations from the start of the question and substituting in our \(\alpha\). Doing this we get: \[ 18 = 30 \times 17 + \beta \text{ (mod 33)}\]
Simplifying this down will give us: \[18=510 +\beta \text{ (mod 33)} \implies -492=\beta \text{ (mod 33)} \implies 3 = \beta \text{ (mod 33)}\]
This gives us our values as \(\alpha = 17\) and \(\beta = 3\).
Hopefully these two examples give you an understanding of how to find an \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) of an affine cipher, however do not worry if this is confusing. You need to remember that this is difficult Maths, so do not worry if you don’t understand it after a few examples. This is Maths that I looked at during my 3rd year of University, and I didn’t fully understand it the first time I saw it. The best advice I can give you is to not give up. There will be plenty of other explanations on the internet and on youtube, so maybe have a look at some of them. Also, you can ask me plenty of questions during our lesson.
Anyway, it’s time for some practice questions.


Practice questions: How to break an affine cipher

Use the Extended Euclidian Algorithm on \(81\) and \(103\) to get an equation in the form \[1 = 81n + 103m\] where \(n\) and \(m\) are integers.
Find the value of \(x\), in the equation \[1=21x \text{ (mod 26)}\] by using the Extended Euclidian Algorithm.
I have an affine cipher using the Ukrainian alphabet. The plaintext letter ‘е’ gets encrypted into the ciphertext letter ‘в’, and the plaintext letter ‘п’ gets encrypted into the ciphertext letter ‘ї’. What value of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) have I used? (Hint: use one of the examples to help you).
I have an affine cipher using the English alphabet. The plaintext letter ‘P’ gets mapped to the ciphertext letter ‘J’, and the plaintext letter ‘S’ gets mapped to the ciphertext letter ‘G’. What value of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) have I used?



Questions to get you thinking

If I told you two different plaintext letters and encrypted them using an affine cipher, and then told you what ciphertext letters they map to, will you always be able to find the value of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) that I used?
Following on from the previous question, I want to always be able to find the \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) used in an affine cipher given two pairs of letters from the plaintext and ciphertext. What property should the number of letters in the alphabet have, so that this is possible?

title: Section 1: Euclids Algorithm
text:
(Difficulty: 3/5)
It’s time to have a little break from the difficult Maths, as this section will mostly be theory.

What is frequency analysis?
Frequency is a method used to decrypt a ciphertext using the frequency of letters. This method will be able to solve any simple substitution cipher (such as the shift cipher and affine cipher), which makes it a powerful tool in classical cryptography.
It works by looking through a ciphertext and counting up how many of each letter show up. We can then compare that to our knowledge of how English is structured, and then guess what each letter could be. Once we have made some guesses, we can then use our knowledge of bigrams and trigrams (we’ll look at these in a moment) to try and fill in any gaps.


What letters show up a lot in English?
The graph below shows you which letters show up the most and the least in the English alphabet. On the x-axis is each letter, and on the y-axis is the probability of that letter being any chosen letter in a text. For example, if I walked into a library, chose a random book, chose a random page from that book, and chose a random letter off that page, then I would have about an $8 % $ chance that the letter I’ve chosen is ‘a’ (the 3rd most common letter).









This graph tells us some interesting things. The first thing to realise, is that the letter ‘e’, is the most common letter in English by quite a significant amount. This means that if you go through a ciphertext, and one letter shows up a lot more than the others, then the chances are that that ciphertext letter represent the plaintext letter ‘e’.
Another interesting fact the graph shows us, is that the letters ‘j’, ‘x’, ‘q’, and ‘z’ are quite rare. So when we are decrypting a ciphertext, and there has been a letter which has only showed up once or twice, then that ciphertext letter probably represents the plaintext letter of either ‘j’, ‘x’, ‘q’ or ‘z’.
I would recommend becoming familiar with the first few most common letters (or you can just come back to the graph), as we will be using that knowledge in the examples.
Before we move onto the next section, it’s only fair that I show you a frequency analysis of the Ukrainian alphabet (also I was interested in it).









If you want to read more about how the data was collected, then I got it from this website https://www.sttmedia.com/characterfrequency-ukrainian. I would also like you to notice that the least common letter only showed up \(0.01 \%\) of the time, which I thought was unusual. When the lesson comes around, remind me to ask you about this.


Bigrams and Trigrams
Before I studied cryptography, I had never heard of these words before. If you ask an English speaking person what a bigram or trigram is, then they will probably have never heard of them. However, they are quite simple. A bigram is two letters wrote next to each other and a trigram is three letters wrote next to each other. Some examples of bigrams are, ‘he’, ‘at’ or ‘qu’. Some examples of trigrams are ‘she’, ‘the’ or ‘pro’. Note that bigrams and trigrams do not have to be words.
Within cryptography, these are very useful, because in a ciphertext you may get three letters which show up next to each other all the time, in which case those three letters probably represent a common trigram. Guessing a bigram or trigram correctly will give you a lot of information, as you will then know 2 or 3 plaintext letters.

Unfortunately, I cannot find a frequency analysis of bigrams and trigrams in the Ukrainian alphabet. If I have some time then I will will conduct a frequency analysis myself, as it is not a difficult thing to do, but it just takes time to make sure everything is correct.

Furthermore, we can see that the most common trigram is ‘QKP’. If ‘P’ represents the letter ‘e’, then the trigram ‘QKP’ probably represents the plaintext ‘the’.
We know that the most common letters in the English alphabet are ‘e’,‘a’ and ‘t’. We already know what ‘e’ and ‘t’ represent, so we need to figure out ‘a’. Sometimes frequency analysis will not work if the ciphertext has a really small amount of letters.

title: Section 1: Shift cipher
text:
(Difficulty: 1/5)
There are a few words we need to learn first to understand the examples. Within cryptography, people send secret messages to each other. We call the messages plaintext. Remember that the plaintext is what humans can understand and read. As we only want the reciever of the message to understand what it says, we need to turn this message into ciphertext. This ciphertext does not make any sense so anyone who intercepts the message will not be able to understand it. To turn the plaintext into ciphertext, we need to encrypt the message. This encryption will be our secret key that only two people will now. Then to turn the ciphertext into plaintext, the reciever needs to decrypt the message. If this does not make any sense, then do not worry. The example below will help you understand.

Example 1: Shift cipher of 1 using English
Imagine we have the english alphabet,





The English Alphabet




I want to use the alphabet to code a secret message. Alice wants to send the word “Svitlo” to Bob. Alice and Bob have agreed to use a shift cipher of 1. This means that each letter in the plaintext (Svitlo) will move one letter to the right. This can be seen in the diagram below:





Diagram explaining a shift cipher of value one.




For “Svitlo”, the S will become a T, the V will become a W and so on. Meaning we get: \[\text{``Svitlo'' in plaintext}=\text{``Twjump'' in ciphertext}\]
So Alice will send “Twjump” to Bob. Bob knows that Alice has shifted every letter one place to the right so to decrypt the message Bob needs to shift every letter one to the left. By doing this Bob, will successfully decrypt Alices message “Svitlo”.
Earlier we learnt 4 words: - Plaintext: The message you want to send someone - Ciphertext: A string of letters that do not make sense. - Encrypt: Use a key to turn the plaintext into ciphertext. - Decrypt: Use a key to turn the ciphertext into plaintext.
We can demonstrate the relationship between these 4 words using the diagram below.





Diagram explaining plaintext, ciphertext, encryption and decryption.




Now we will look at another example using the Ukrainian alphabet.


Example 2: Shift cipher of 3 using Ukrainian
We will now do a similar example using the Ukrainian alphabet. Suppose Yuliya wanted to send the message “привіт” to Daria using a shift cipher of 3. We can use the Ukrainian alphabet to help encrypt the message.





Ukrainian alphabet.




We are now using a shift cipher of 3, meaning that for each letter we will shift it 3 places to the right. Now we can draw the same diagram as we did in the last question, where the red arrows tell us where each letter maps to.









Notice that I did not draw in all off the red arrows, lots of arrows will make it look confusing and messy. This is why we can use a slightly better diagram. The diagram below has the normal alphabet on top and where each letter is mapped to on the bottom. In other words, we will have the plaintext on the top, and the ciphertext on the bottom.









This diagram makes it very easy to convert between the plaintext and the ciphertext. Using this diagram we can see that encrypting “привіт”, will give us “туйдкх . Unfortunately, I do not speak ukrainian, but I hope that”туйдкх” is not a word and does not make sense by itself. This means that: \[\text{``привіт" in plaintext}=\text{``туйдкх" in ciphertext}\]”
To decrypt the message, you can simply use the diagram the other way around and it will give you the plaintext back.


Practice questions
Hopefully by now you have a basic understanding of what plaintext, ciphertext, encryption and decryption is. We will now put your knowledge to the test with a few practice questions. Also, for now we will only be using a shift cipher, but in the next lesson we will be looking at a different cipher. If you are interested and want to look at it in advance then it is called an affine cipher (but we will look at it next week anyway).

(Difficulty: 2/5)
This next section is important for studying cryptography, so if you have never seen this before, I encourage you to take your time to make sure you understand this well.
Modular arithmetic is sometimes called “clock arithmetic” because of how we can use a clock to explain it. Imagine we have a 12 hour clock, where the 12 has been replaced by a zero. It would look something like this:









We can see that this clock tells us that the time is 2 o’clock. If wait 8 hours, then the clock will show 10 o’clock, which can be seen below:









This is easy to understand, as \(2+8=10\). But what happens if we wait another 8 hours?
from IPython.display import Image, display display(Image(filename=‘Clock mod example 3.png’, height=350, width=800))
As you can see, waiting another 8 hours means it will go to 6 o’clock. On this clock we cannot have any number which is 12 or greater. This means when we go past the number 11, we have to take away 12 until we get a number between zero and eleven inclusive. So when we add 8 hours the seconds time what we are doing is: \(10+8=18\), but because we know that \(18\) is 12 or greater, then we have to take away 12. When we take away 12 we get \(18-12=6\), which is why the clock shows 6 o’clock. We will now look at a spinner which only has 4 numbers.









We can see that we now have a spinner with only 4 numbers (or if you want then you can imagine it to be some sort of Alien clock). The spinner is currently showing the number 2. If we moved the hand on the spinner 3 times clockwise, then it would end up on the number 1. This can be shown below:









In this case, the calculation we are doing is \(2+3=5\). However the clock does not show the number \(5\) meaning we need to take away \(4\) until we get a number which does appear on the clock. Hence, we do \(5-4=1\) so the clock shows the number \(1\).
Now we need to translate the clock and spinner into Mathematics. When a clock has 12 numbers, we say that we are doing the calculations\(\mod 12\). Writing out the example with the clock Mathematically would look like this: \[2+8=10 \text{ (mod } 12)\] \[10+8=18 \equiv 6 \text{ (mod } 12)\]
In the second example with the spinner (which has 4 numbers), we would write: \[2+3=5 \equiv 1\text{ (mod }4)\]
Now before some practice questions, we will look at some examples.

Example 1
Calculate \(13 + 21 \text{ (mod 26)}\):
First, we will calculate \(13+21\), which will give \(34\). \(34\) is greater than 26 meaning we need to take away 26 until we get a number between 0 and 25 inclusive. \(34-26=8\), meaning that: \[13+21 \equiv 8 \text{ (mod 26)}\]


Example 2
Calculate \(7 \times 5 \text{ (mod 35)}\):
First, we will calculate \(7 \times 5\) which will give \(35\). An important fact to remember is that \(n \equiv 0 \text{ (mod n)}\). This might be a little confusing, but if you think about the clock we saw earlier, it had \(12\) numbers on but only went up to \(11\) as zero was on the clock instead of the \(12\). This means that: \[ 7 \times 5 \equiv 0 \text{ (mod 35)}\]


Practice questions
I’m hoping that this section has not been too difficult for you, however it is still useful to have a go at some practice questions.

Calculate \(9+6 \text{ (mod 11)}\)
Calculate \(3+7 \text{ (mod 5)}\)
Calculate \(6 \times 8 \text{ (mod 20)}\)



Questions to get you thinking

Calculate \(n^n \text{ (mod n)}\)
Try using addition and subtraction under (mod 2). Do you notice anything interesting when using addition and subtraction with the same numbers? Can you explain why this is happening?

text:
(Difficulty: 2/5)
Within this section we will combine what we have learnt in the previous two sections. This will help you to understand cryptography in a more mathematical way. The first step will be to convert our alphabet into numbers, which can be seen in the diagram below:









As each letter now corresponds to a number, we can introduce a new formula: \[ c = p + s \text{ (mod 26)}\] where \(c\) represents the ciphertext, \(p\) represents the plaintext and \(s\) represents the shift. Using this formula, if we wanted to encrypt the plaintext letter “r” using a shift ciphper of 5, then we would first see what number “r” corresponds to. We can see that “r” is represented by 17, so to get the ciphertext we do \(p + s = 17 + 5 = 22\). We can see that \(22\) represents to letter “w”, so using a shift cipher of 5 “r” will get encrypted to be “w”.
Now we will use these numbers to encrypt the word “Svitlo” with a shift cipher of 3.

Example 1
To encrypt “Svitlo” with a shift cipher of 3, we first need do convert all the letters into numbers. So we get, \[\text{``Svitlo"}= 18,21,8,19,11,14\] Then we use the formula and add 3 to these numbers. So we get, \[c=p+s \rightarrow 18+3,21+3,8+3,19+3,11+3,14+3 = 21,24,11,22,14,17\] Now that we have our ciphertext, we will convert it back into letters to give \[21,24,11,22,14,17 = \text{``Vylwor"}\]
Now that we have looked at that example, you might be thinking Why have we bothered to turn the letters into numbers? We can easily do a shift cipher without numbers!, and you would very correct to think this. For a shift cipher it is rather easy to see how the letters will be encrypted, however in future lessons we will look at more complicated ciphers which are not so easy to understand. I have shown you how to turn the letters into numbers with a simple example (shift cipher), so that when we look at harder ciphers you will be able to understand them quicker.
Another reason why we use formulas in encryption is to easily see how to decrypt a message. If we have just recieved the ciphertext from a message, then we can convert it back to the plaintext by rearranging our formula: \[ c = p + s \text{ (mod 26)} \implies p = c - s \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We will now use this idea in an example.


Example 2
You have recived the ciphertext, “ъсaблвр” which has been created using a shift cipher of 15. What is the plaintext?
Before we start this question, I have to point out the obvious which is that for this example we will be using the Ukrainian alphabet instead of the English alphabet. This means that any calculations we do will have to be in \(\text{(mod 33)}\), because the Ukrainian alphabet has 33 letters in. With that in mind, we can start by converting our ciphertext into numbers. We will do this using the following table:









From this table, we can see that: \[\text{``ъсaблвр''}=30,21,0,1,15,2,20\]
Now that we have our ciphertext as numbers, we can use the formula \(p = c - s \text{ (mod 33)}\) to convert from the ciphertext to the plaintext.
\[30-15,21-15,0-15,1-15,15-15,2-15,20-15 = 15,6,18,19,20,5 \text{ (mod 33)}\] Now we can convert these numbers (which represent our plaintext) back into letters to find out what the message was. \[15,6,18,19,20,5=\text{``Леопард''}\]
Now we will finish this weeks lesson with some practice questions.

title: Section 1: Prime factor decomposition
text:
(Difficulty 2/5)
In Mathematics, you have probably heard of a prime number before. Prime numbers are numbers which can only be divided by one and itself. Examples of prime numbers include: \(2,3,5,7,11,13,...\)
An example of a number which is not prime would be \(15\), because we know that \(15= 5 \times 3\). Every number is either a prime number, or is made by multiplying prime numbers together. You can think of prime numbers as being the building blocks of every other number. As prime numbers are so important, then it’s useful to be able to find out what prime numbers are used to make up a number. This is called prime factor decomposition, and we will look at an example now.
Lastly, it is important to remember that \(1\) is not a prime number. The definition of a prime number is that the number can only be divided by one AND itself. The keyword here is ‘and’, because this implies that a prime number has to have exactly two factors. However, when we look at the number \(1\), we can see that it only has one as a factor, as \(1 = 1 \times 1\). As the number \(1\) only has one factor, then it is not prime.

Example 1
Find the prime factor decomposition of \(150\). With this example I have created step by step images showing you what to do. I will talk through each of the images so you can follow along and see what is happening at each step.

For the first step, all we have to do is simply write the number at the top of the page.
In step 2, we have picked two numbers that multiply to give \(150\). I have chosen \(3\) and \(50\).
We then look to see if any of these numbers are prime. As \(3\) is a prime number, we put a red circle around it to show that it’s then end of that branch.
We then repeat the process and split 50 into two numbers which multiply to give \(50\). I chose \(25\) and \(2\).
As \(2\) is prime, we put a red circle around it.
We then split \(25\) into two numbers which multiply to give \(25\). The only two numbers which do that are going to be \(5\) and \(5\).
As 5 is prime, we put red circles around both the number \(5\)’s.
As every branch finishes with a number in a red circle, then our tree is complete. We can write down every number in a red circle and say that they will multiply to give the number at the very top. In this case, \(150 = 5^2 \times 2 \times 3\). Note that we have \(5^2\) because the number 5 appears twice.


  
  
    ◀ Back
    Step 1 of 8
    Next ▶
  





Now we have found all of the prime factors that make up \(150\). We will look at another example, just to make sure that you’re happy with it.


Example 2
Find the prime factor decomposition of \(144\). This is exactly the same as the last example only using a different number. I will now talk through each step included in the diagram below.

First step is to write the starting number at the top of the page.
Then we choose two numbers which, when multiplied together, give the starting number. We draw arrows to these and write them below, for this case I chose \(8\) and \(18\).
We can notice that both \(8\) and \(18\) are not prime meaning that we need to repeat our previous step and pick two numbers which multiply to give \(8\) and two numbers which multiply to give \(18\). I chose \(2\) and \(4\), and \(2\) and \(9\).
We can notice that \(2\) is prime so we circle them.
We then split \(9\) up into \(3 \times 3\) and \(4\) into \(2 \times 2\).
As both \(3\) and \(2\) are prime, we circle them.
Now that the tree is complete and every branch ends in a red circle, then we can multiply all the numbers in the red circles together to give us our starting number. As \(2\) appears 4 times, and \(3\) appears twice, then we have \(144=2^4 \times 3^2\)


  
  
    ◀ Back 
    Step 1 of 8 
    Next ▶
  





Hopefully you now understand how to draw a factor tree to find the prime decomposition of a number. We will practice your new skills using some questions!

title: Section 1: Prime factor decomposition
text:
(Difficulty 2/5)
In our previous section, we looked at prime numbers which you have probably heard of before in school. Now I want to introduce you to something that you have probably never seen before, but you will need it to understand our next cipher, so make sure you understand it!

What are coprime numbers?
Coprime numbers are a pair of numbers which do not share any prime factors with each other. For example, \(16\) and \(21\) are coprime, because if we look at the prime factor decompositions, then \(16=2^4\) and \(21=3 \times 7\). As you can see, these do not share any prime factors meaning they are coprime.
However, if we wanted to see if \(21\) and \(35\) are coprime, then we first need to split them up into their prime factor decomposition. This gives us \(21 = 7 \times 3\) and \(35 = 7 \times 5\). As you can see, both \(21\) and \(35\) share the number \(7\) as one of their prime factors, meaning that \(21\) and \(35\) are not coprime.


Coprime numbers in terms of gcd
Another way of defining a coprime numbers is by saying ‘Two numbers are coprime if their greatest common divisor is equal to one’. Mathematically, we write that two numbers (we can call these numbers \(a\) and \(b\)) are coprime if \(gcd(a,b)=1\), where \(gcd(a,b)\) means the greatest common divisor of \(a\) and \(b\).
Now just in case you have never heard of the greatest common divisor before, here is the definition. The greatest common divisor of two numbers is the largest number which perfectly divides the two numbers. For example, the greatest common divisor between \(24\) and \(60\) is equal to \(12\), so we would write \(gcd(24,60)=12\).
To find the greatest common divisor, we look at the shared prime factors between the two numbers. We can see that the factor trees of \(24\) and \(60\) are, \(24=2^3 \times 3\) and \(60=2^2 \times 3 \times 5\). If we were to put these numbers into a Venn diagram, we would get:









We can see that in the middle of the Venn diagram, we have \(2, 2, 3\). When we multiply these together, we get the greatest common divisor. We can double check our answer and calculate that \(2 \times 2 \times 3 = 12\) just like we expected!
When you use both of these definitions for a coprime number, you will see that they mean the same thing, only they’ve been said differently. Using the first definition, we can see that two numbers can only be coprime if they do not share any prime factors, and if two numbers do not share any prime factors, then their greatest common divisor must be equal to zero.
Like usual, we are going to have a look at an example before doing any practice questions.


Example 1
Find the greatest common divisor of \(52\) and \(45\). Using this information, are they coprime?
The first thing we need to do is find the prime factor decompositions of \(52\) and \(45\). I’m not going to do this for you as we have already done it in the last section. But once you write out the factor trees, you should get: \(52 = 2^2 \times 13\) and \(45 = 3^2 \times 5\).
The next step is to put these into a Venn diagram:









We can see that \(45\) and \(52\) do not share any prime factors, meaning that their greatest common divisor is equal to \(1\). We can write \(gcd(45,52)=1\). As \(45\) and \(52\) do not share any prime factors, then they must be coprime.
Hopefully that example makes sense to you, but if it doesn’t then you can always ask me in the next lesson. Now it’s time for some practice questions.

text:
(Difficulty 3/5)
This lesson course is a cryptography course, and considering we have not done any cryptography in the last two sections, I think it is best that we look at a new cipher. For the sake of you not having to flick between this weeks lesson and last weeks lesson, I’m going to include the English and Ukrainian alphabet here, as you will need it later.


















Last week we looked at a shift cipher, where you add a ‘shift’ onto the plaintext to change it into ciphertext. With an affine cipher, we do two changes to the plaintext. We first multiply the plaintext by some number, then add a shift onto our multiplied plaintext. An affine ciper (for the English alphabet) is defined as follows:
Choose a number \(\alpha\) such that \(gcd(26,\alpha)=1\) then choose some number \(\beta\). The cipher sends each plaintext letter \(p\) to ciphertext letter \(C= \alpha p + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\)
Time to look at some examples using this cipher.

Example 1
Encrypt the plaintext letter ‘H’ using an affine cipher with \(\alpha = 5\) and \(\beta = 9\).
The first step will be to convert the letter ‘H’ into a number. Using the alphabet above, we can see that: \[H=7\]
Now we can use our cipher. First we multiply our plaintext by our \(\alpha\), then we add our \(\beta\). This means we will have: \[5 \times 7 +9 = 35 + 9 = 44 \equiv 18 \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Then to convert \(18\) into our ciphertext, we can check the alphabet above. We can see that ‘S’=18. This gives us our final answer, so we know that using an affine cipher with \(\alpha = 5\) and \(\beta = 9\) the plaintext letter ‘H’ will be encrypted into the ciphertext letter ‘S’.


Example 2
Encrypt the Ukrainian word ‘вівця’ using an affine cipher with \(\alpha = 26\) and \(\beta = 3\). Remember that because we are now using the Ukrainian alphabet, all calculations need to be done \(\text{mod 33}\).
First, we will convert our word into numbers. We can use the alphabet above to give: \[\text{в}=2, \text{і}=11, \text{ц}=26, \text{я}=32\]
Once we have our numbers, then we can use the cipher. We will get: \[2 \times 26+3=52+3=55 \equiv 22 \text{ (mod 33)}\] \[11 \times 26+3=286+3=289 \equiv 25 \text{ (mod 33)}\] \[26 \times 26+3=676+3=679 \equiv 19 \text{ (mod 33)}\] \[32 \times 26+3=832+3=835 \equiv 7 \text{ (mod 33)}\]
Now we can convert these numbers back into letters. Using the Ukrainian alphabet above we will get: \[22=\text{т},25=\text{х},19=\text{п},10=\text{и}\]
When we encrypt the work ‘вівця’ using an affine cipher with \(\alpha = 26\) and \(\beta = 3\) then we get the ciphertext ‘тхтпи’.


Example 3
I have encrypted an English word using an affine cipher with \(\alpha = 5\) and \(\beta = 10\). The ciphertext is ‘QKBER’. What is the English word that I encrypted?
The first step is to convert the ciphertext into numbers. Using the alphabet we can see that: \[Q=16,K=10,B=1,E=4,R=17\]
We know that for an affine cipher: \[\text{Ciphertext} = \alpha \times \text{Plaintext} + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Rearranging this will give: \[ \text{Ciphertext} - \beta = \alpha \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We need to be a little bit clever for this next step, as we need to make sure that the value we calculate for the Plaintext is an integer. For the first letter (Q), we will do: \[16-10=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 6=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We can see here that if we divided both sides of the equation by \(5\), then we would not get an integer value for \(\text{Plaintext}\). This means we need to keep on adding 26 onto the left hand side of the equation until we get a multiple of \(5\). We can add \(6\) onto multiples of \(26\) until we find a multiple of \(5\): \[26+6=32\] \[52+6=58\] \[78+6=84\] \[104+6=110\]
We can see that \(110\) is a multiple of \(5\), meaning we can write:\[6=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 110 = 5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Now we are able to divide both sides of the equation by \(5\), to give:\[110 = 5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 22 = \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We can see that \(22\) corresponds to W. Meaning that the first letter of our plaintext is W. We can now use the same method to find the remaining letters for our plaintext.
For our next letter K: \[10-10=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 0=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
This means that \(\text{Plaintext}\) must be equal to zero. We do not need to start adding 26. As \(\text{Plaintext}\) is equal to zero, then the next letter in our decoded message must be A.
For our third letter B: \[1-10=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies -9=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
We can add multiples of 26 onto the left hand side of this equation to get: \[95=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Dividing both sides by 5 we will get:\[95=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 19 = \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
So our third letter in our decoded work will be T.
For our fourth letter E:
\[4-10=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies -6=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
For this equation we can see that we only need to add 26 once to the left hand side to get a multiple of 5. Doing this, we will get: \[-6=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 20=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 4 = \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
This means that our fourth decoded letter is E. Note how for this specific letter, the ciphertext is equal to the plaintext.
For our final letter R:
\[17-10=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 7=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
By adding multiples of 26 to the left hand side of the equation, we will get:\[7=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 85=5 \times \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)} \implies 17 = \text{Plaintext} \text{ (mod 26)}\]
This means that our final decoded letter is R.
Our last step is to put all of our decoded letters together. By doing that, we can see that the decrypted message is WATER.
Now that we have finished our last example for affine ciphers, it is time for some practice questions. I would like to remind you that this is difficult Maths, as you are using concepts which you likely have never seen before. So do not expect to get it all correct first try. My best advice would be to just have a go! Making mistakes is the best way to learn, and if you have any questions then you can ask me in the lesson (or put a message on the google classroom or ask one of your classmates).

title: Section 1: Prime factor decomposition
text:
Extension work
I am including this section to answer a question which I had when I first learnt about this topic. Please note that this section is not needed to understand any of the content further on in this course, it is only here in case any of you are interested in learning a little bit more Maths. The question I want to answer is: ‘Why does \(\alpha\) have to be coprime to the number of letters in the alphabet that we’re using?’ 
The first thing we need to ask ourselves is, ‘Why does a cipher work?’, and one of the reasons why a cipher works is because it maps each letter from the plaintext onto one unique letter in the ciphertext. In other words, no two letters in the plaintext will map to the same letter in the ciphertext. If this did happen then it would be impossible to decrypt the ciphertext, as you would not know which letter from the plaintext was used. For example, imagine a cipher mapped the letter ‘A’ and the letter ‘G’ to the letter ‘K’. If I then gave you the letter ‘K’ and asked you which letter in the plaintext was encrypted to give you ‘K’, you would have no idea because it could be either ‘A’ or ‘G’.
So, we know that two letters in the ciphertext cannot be equal to each other if they have come from different plaintext letters. Now to answer our question of why \(\alpha\) has to be coprime, we are going to use a technique called proof by contradiction. If we want to prove that \(\alpha\) has to be coprime with 26 (for the English alphabet), then we need to prove it is impossible to have a valid cipher when \(\alpha\) is not coprime with 26. I know that this might be confusing if you have never seen proof by contradiction before, so if you haven’t, then I would recommend reading about it or asking me in the lesson. Proof by contradiction is a very powerful tool, so if you plan on doing a lot of Maths in the future, then I recommend learning about it now.
Anyway, back to our proof. Imagine we have some affine cipher with an \(\alpha\) which is not coprime to 26. We can now choose two values from the plaintext \(n\) and \(m\) (remember these represent numbers, and not letters). If these did represent the same letters in the ciphertext, then we would get: \[ \alpha n + \beta \equiv \alpha m + \beta \text{ (mod 26)}\]
Immediately we can take away \(\beta\) from both sides to get: \[ \alpha n \equiv \alpha m \text{ (mod 26)}\]
If we know that \(\alpha\) is coprime with 26, then there will be some value of \(\alpha\) which is a factor of 26. There must also be some value of \(n\) such that \(\alpha n\) is equal to a multiple of 26 (for example, \(\alpha\) = 2 and \(n\) =13). This means that if \(\alpha n\) is equal to a multiple of 26, then we will get: \[\alpha n \equiv \alpha m \text{(mod 26)} \implies 0 \equiv \alpha m \text{ (mod 26)}\]
This equation is true when \(n=m\), which is good because if \(n=m\) then we have the same letter in the plaintext being mapped to the same letter in the ciphertext. However, this equation is also true for \(m=0\), which will break our cipher as it means that two different letters in the plaintext are being mapped to the same letter in the ciphertext. We know that \(n\) is not equal to zero as we said earlier that \(\alpha n\) is a multiple of 26, which cannot be true if \(n\) is zero. Therefore, in order to have a valid affine cipher, \(\alpha\) has to be coprime with 26.
